question: Real wasabi is expensive and hard to grow. Most of the green paste served with sushi outside Japan is made mainly from which cheaper root, dyed green?
source_excerpt: A common substitute is a mixture of horseradish, mustard, starch, and green food coloring or spinach powder.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the green blob on their sushi plate is wasabi. Learning it is usually a dyed impostor is a small everyday shock, and the burn on the nose gives a solid clue.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia and product ingredient lists confirm that imitation wasabi outside Japan is mainly horseradish (plus mustard, starch and green coloring); no newer development contradicts this.

explanation: Imitation wasabi is mostly horseradish with a little mustard and green colouring. Genuine wasabi is often grated fresh at the table and has a milder, sweeter heat.

question: When South Korea sent its first astronaut into space in 2008, scientists had spent years developing a space-safe version of which spicy fermented cabbage dish for her to take along?
source_excerpt: Scientists at the Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute in Daejeon say they have cooked up a special kimchi for space travel

extra.why_interesting: A nation spent years of research making its signature side dish safe for orbit. It is a funny, human detail, and the stem gives clear footholds: Korea, fermented cabbage.
extra.verification_notes: Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute scientists developed space kimchi for Yi So-yeon's 2008 Soyuz flight as Korea's first astronaut; no newer event overturns this (https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.312.5774.667b).

explanation: Korean food scientists sterilised the kimchi so its live bacteria could not misbehave in orbit. Yi So-yeon took it to the International Space Station.

question: True or false: the man who designed the Pringles crisp can asked for his ashes to be buried in one, and his family honoured the request.
source_excerpt: Baur's children said they honoured his request to bury him in one of the cans by placing part of his cremated remains in a Pringles container

extra.why_interesting: It sounds exactly like an internet hoax, so many players will bet 'False'. The truth is stranger and oddly touching.
extra.verification_notes: Snopes, citing a 2008 AP report, confirms Baur requested burial in a Pringles can and his children honoured it by burying part of his ashes in one; no newer development contradicts this.

explanation: True. When Fredric Baur died in 2008, his children stopped at a pharmacy on the way to the funeral home, bought a can of Pringles and buried part of his ashes in it.

question: Caesar salad has nothing to do with Julius Caesar. It is named after an Italian restaurateur who first served it in the 1920s in which country?
source_excerpt: Place of origin: Mexico; Region or state: Tijuana, Baja California; Created by: Caesar Cardini; Invented: 1924

extra.why_interesting: The name points to Rome and the chef was Italian, so players reach for Italy. The real birthplace is a Mexican border town that served Prohibition-era Americans.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia, Britannica and National Geographic all place the 1920s origin of Caesar salad at Caesar Cardini's restaurant in Tijuana, Mexico; no newer development contradicts this.

explanation: Caesar Cardini created it at his restaurant in Tijuana, just across the border from Prohibition-era America. Thirsty Californians drove down to eat and drink there.

question: Saffron, the world's most expensive spice by weight, is made from tiny threads plucked by hand from the centre of which purple flower?
source_excerpt: Saffron is a spice derived from the flower of Crocus sativus, commonly known as the 'saffron crocus'.

extra.why_interesting: Many people use saffron without knowing it comes from a garden flower they would recognise. The hand-picking detail explains the price.
extra.verification_notes: Saffron is derived from the hand-harvested stigmas of the purple Crocus sativus flower, and it is widely described as the most expensive spice by weight; nothing newer contradicts this.

explanation: Each saffron crocus gives just three red stigmas. Making a single kilogram of saffron takes well over a hundred thousand flowers.

question: Which spice comes from a Mexican orchid and could only be grown widely abroad after a 12-year-old boy on the island of Réunion worked out how to pollinate its flowers by hand in 1841?
source_excerpt: that method was discovered by an enslaved 12-year-old Black boy named Edmond Albius in 1841 on the tiny volcanic island of Réunion

extra.why_interesting: Vanilla feels like the most ordinary flavour there is, yet its global supply rests on an orchid and on one child's technique. The clues (Mexico, orchid, Madagascar) let a thoughtful player get there.
extra.verification_notes: Vanilla is a Mexican orchid, and Edmond Albius, aged 12, devised hand pollination on Réunion in 1841, which made wide cultivation outside Mexico possible.

explanation: Edmond Albius's method is still used today, because outside Mexico the orchid lacks its natural pollinators. Every flower on the plantations of Madagascar is pollinated by hand.
